chapter.name: Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry
chapter.blurb: This chapter extends coordinate geometry from the plane to space. It sets up three mutually perpendicular coordinate axes and coordinate planes, shows how every point in space gets an ordered triplet (x, y, z) and how the signs of the coordinates fix one of eight octants. It then derives the distance formula between two points in space and uses it to test collinearity, identify triangles and parallelograms, and write equations of sets of points.

scope_in.item: Explain why three numbers (perpendicular distances from three mutually perpendicular planes) are needed to locate a point in space
Name the x, y and z-axes (X'OX, Y'OY, Z'OZ), the origin, and the XY, YZ and ZX coordinate planes, and say which axes lie in which plane and along which axis two planes meet
Use the sign convention for directed distances: above/below the XY-plane, right/left of the ZX-plane, in front of/behind the YZ-plane
State that the coordinate planes divide space into eight octants, and name them by half-axes (XOYZ, X'OYZ, X'OY'Z, XOY'Z, XOYZ', X'OYZ', X'OY'Z', XOY'Z') with their numbers I to VIII

Find the coordinates (x, y, z) of a point from the construction PM perpendicular to the XY-plane and ML perpendicular to the x-axis (OL = x, LM = y, MP = z), or from planes through P parallel to the coordinate planes meeting the axes at A, B, C; and locate a point from a given triplet
Read x, y, z as the perpendicular distances of a point from the YZ, ZX and XY planes

Write the form of the coordinates of the origin, of a point on each axis and of a point in each coordinate plane, and find the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a coordinate plane (as in Example 1)
Use Table 11.1 of signs of coordinates to name the octant of a given point, or the signs for a given octant
State, follow the derivation of, and use the distance formula PQ = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2 + (z2 - z1)^2), including the distance from the origin sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)

Use distances to show three points are collinear (sum of two distances equals the third), to test whether a triangle is isosceles, equilateral or right angled, and to show four points form a parallelogram that is or is not a rectangle (opposite sides equal, diagonals compared)
Find the equation of a set of points P(x, y, z) given a distance condition, such as PA = PB or PA^2 + PB^2 = constant

concepts.name: Coordinate axes, coordinate planes and octants
concepts.description: The three mutually perpendicular axes and planes of the rectangular coordinate system in space, the sign convention for directed distances, and the eight octants named by their half-axes.
concepts.idea: Three mutually perpendicular planes through a point O meet along three mutually perpendicular lines, the x, y and z-axes, and cut space into eight parts.
concepts.rule: The planes XOY, YOZ and ZOX are the XY, YZ and ZX-planes. Distances are positive above the XY-plane (along OZ), to the right of the ZX-plane (along OY) and in front of the YZ-plane (along OX). The octants XOYZ, X'OYZ, X'OY'Z, XOY'Z, XOYZ', X'OYZ', X'OY'Z', XOY'Z' are denoted I to VIII.
concepts.example: A point behind the YZ-plane, to the right of the ZX-plane and above the XY-plane is in the octant X'OYZ, which is octant II.

Octant I is named XOYZ. Octants II, III and IV also lie above the XY-plane. Write the names of octants II, III and IV and describe how the name changes from each octant to the next.
questions.a: Octant II is X'OYZ, octant III is X'OY'Z and octant IV is XOY'Z. questions.q: A room is modelled with its floor as the XY-plane and two adjacent walls as the YZ-plane and the ZX-plane, the corner where all three meet being the origin O. The room occupies the octant XOYZ. (a) Which coordinate axis runs along the vertical line in which the two walls meet? (b) Along which coordinate axis does the floor meet the wall that is the ZX-plane? (c) A second room lies directly below this one, on the other side of the floor. Name the octant it occupies by its half-axes.
questions.a: (a) The two walls are the YZ-plane and the ZX-plane; both contain the z-axis, so they meet along the z-axis. (b) The floor is the XY-plane and the wall is the ZX-plane; both contain the x-axis, so they meet along the x-axis. (c) Going below the XY-plane changes only the direction OZ to OZ', so the room below occupies the octant XOYZ'.
s: States that the two walls meet along the z-axis
States that the floor and the ZX-plane wall meet along the x-axis
Names the lower room's octant as XOYZ', with only OZ changed to OZ'

questions.q: Consider these statements about the sign convention for distances in space. (I) Distances measured to the right of the ZX-plane along OY are taken as positive. (II) Distances measured to the back of the YZ-plane along OX' are taken as positive. Which is or are correct?

A student argues: 'Two coordinate axes divide a plane into 4 quadrants, so three coordinate axes must divide space into 6 parts.' Analyse this argument. State what actually divides the space, how many parts are formed, and explain the count using the two sides of each coordinate plane.
questions.a: The space is divided by the three coordinate planes (XY, YZ and ZX), not by the three axes, which are only lines. Each coordinate plane has two sides: above or below the XY-plane, in front of or behind the YZ-plane, to the right or left of the ZX-plane. A part of space is fixed by choosing one side for each of the three planes, giving 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 parts. So the space is divided into 8 octants, not 6.
s: States that the three coordinate planes, not the axes, divide the space
Explains that each of the three planes has two sides and a part is fixed by one choice of side per plane
Concludes 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 octants, so the claim of 6 parts is wrong

questions.q: Ravi says: 'The octant X'OYZ' lies above the XY-plane, because its name contains the letter Z.' Is Ravi right? Justify your answer by describing where this octant lies relative to all three coordinate planes.
questions.a: Ravi is wrong. The name contains Z', which stands for the direction OZ', and distances along OZ' are measured downwards from the XY-plane. So the octant X'OYZ' lies below the XY-plane; it is also behind the YZ-plane (OX') and to the right of the ZX-plane (OY).
s: Says Ravi is wrong because Z' means the direction OZ', which is below the XY-plane
Describes the octant as behind the YZ-plane, to the right of the ZX-plane and below the XY-plane

questions.q: Make up your own description of the position of a point, using the words in front of or behind the YZ-plane, right or left of the ZX-plane and above or below the XY-plane, with distances of your own choice, so that the point lies in the octant X'OY'Z. State the sign of each of the three directed distances and explain why your point is in that octant.
questions.a: One possible answer: the point is 3 units behind the YZ-plane, 2 units to the left of the ZX-plane and 4 units above the XY-plane. Behind the YZ-plane is along OX', so that distance is negative; left of the ZX-plane is along OY', so that distance is negative; above the XY-plane is along OZ, so that distance is positive. The half-axes used are OX', OY' and OZ, so the point lies in the octant X'OY'Z. (Any distances work, provided the point is behind, to the left and above.)
s: Gives a description that places the point behind the YZ-plane, left of the ZX-plane and above the XY-plane
States the signs as negative, negative and positive for the distances along the x, y and z directions
Explains that the half-axes OX', OY' and OZ give the octant X'OY'Z

concepts.name: Coordinates of a point in space
concepts.description: Associating an ordered triplet (x, y, z) with a point, reading the coordinates as perpendicular distances from the coordinate planes, and the special forms of points on the axes and in the coordinate planes.
concepts.idea: Every point in space corresponds to exactly one ordered triplet (x, y, z) of real numbers, and every triplet to exactly one point.
concepts.rule: x, y and z are the perpendicular distances of the point from the YZ, ZX and XY-planes. The origin is (0, 0, 0); points on the x, y, z-axes are (x, 0, 0), (0, y, 0), (0, 0, z); points in the XY, YZ, ZX-planes are (x, y, 0), (0, y, z), (x, 0, z).
concepts.example: For P(2, 4, 5), the foot of the perpendicular on the ZX-plane has no distance along OY, so it is (2, 0, 5).

questions.a: Meena is wrong. The point (0, 3, 0) has x = 0 and z = 0, so it lies on the y-axis. Since x = 0 it is in the YZ-plane, and since z = 0 it is in the XY-plane, so it lies in two coordinate planes. It is not in the ZX-plane because its y-coordinate is not 0.

questions.a: One possible answer: (0, 0, 5) is on the z-axis because its x and y coordinates are both 0. (2, 3, 0) is in the XY-plane because its z-coordinate is 0, and it is on no axis because only one coordinate is 0. (1, 2, 3) is in no coordinate plane because none of its coordinates is 0.
s: Gives a point of the form (0, 0, z) with z not 0, justified by x = y = 0
Gives a point of the form (x, y, 0) with x and y not 0, justified by only z = 0
Gives a point with all three coordinates non-zero, justified by no coordinate being 0

concepts.name: Signs of coordinates and the octant of a point
concepts.description: Using the table of signs of x, y and z in the eight octants to name the octant of a point or the signs in a given octant.
concepts.idea: The signs of the three coordinates of a point decide the octant in which it lies.
concepts.rule: Signs of (x, y, z): I (+, +, +), II (-, +, +), III (-, -, +), IV (+, -, +), V (+, +, -), VI (-, +, -), VII (-, -, -), VIII (+, -, -). Octants I to IV have z positive; V to VIII repeat the same x, y signs with z negative.
concepts.example: (-3, 1, 2) has signs (-, +, +), so it is in octant II; (-3, 1, -2) has signs (-, +, -), so it is in octant VI.

questions.a: (4, 2, -5) has signs (+, +, -), which is octant V. (-2, -4, -7) has signs (-, -, -), which is octant VII.
s: States (4, 2, -5) has signs (+, +, -) and lies in octant V
States (-2, -4, -7) has signs (-, -, -) and lies in octant VII

questions.q: Three points are A(5, -2, 4), B(-5, -2, 4) and C(-5, 2, -4). (a) Name the octant in which each point lies. (b) Between A and B only one coordinate changes sign; name the coordinate plane that therefore lies between A and B. (c) State how many coordinates change sign from B to C and whether B and C are on the same side of the YZ-plane.
questions.a: (a) A has signs (+, -, +), octant IV; B has signs (-, -, +), octant III; C has signs (-, +, -), octant VI. (b) From A to B only x changes sign, and x is the distance from the YZ-plane, so the YZ-plane lies between A and B. (c) From B to C the y and z coordinates change sign, that is two coordinates; x is negative for both, so B and C are on the same side of (behind) the YZ-plane.
s: Names the octants IV, III and VI for A, B and C
States that the YZ-plane lies between A and B because only x changes sign
States that two coordinates (y and z) change from B to C and that both points are on the same side of the YZ-plane

questions.q: Consider these statements about the signs of coordinates in the octants. (I) If the y-coordinate of a point is positive, the point cannot lie in octant III. (II) The x-coordinate of a point is positive in octants I, IV, V and VIII. Which is or are correct?

The coordinates of a point P(x, y, z) satisfy xy < 0 and z > 0. (a) List the possible sign patterns of (x, y, z). (b) Name the octants in which P can lie. (c) If it is also known that x > 0, in which octant does P lie?
questions.a: (a) xy < 0 means x and y have opposite signs, and z is positive, so the patterns are (+, -, +) and (-, +, +). (b) (+, -, +) is octant IV and (-, +, +) is octant II, so P lies in octant II or octant IV. (c) If x > 0 the pattern is (+, -, +), so P lies in octant IV.
s: Lists the two patterns (+, -, +) and (-, +, +)
Names the possible octants as II and IV
Concludes octant IV when x > 0

questions.q: Kiran says: 'The points (-2, 6, 4) and (-2, -6, 4) lie in the same octant, because both are behind the YZ-plane and both are above the XY-plane.' Evaluate Kiran's claim.
questions.a: Kiran is wrong. An octant is fixed by the signs of all three coordinates, not two. (-2, 6, 4) has signs (-, +, +) and lies in octant II, while (-2, -6, 4) has signs (-, -, +) and lies in octant III. Their y-coordinates have opposite signs, so they are on opposite sides of the ZX-plane.
s: States that the octant depends on the signs of all three coordinates and the y signs differ
Identifies the octants as II and III, so the claim is wrong

questions.q: Create three points, each at perpendicular distances 1, 2 and 3 units from the YZ-plane, the ZX-plane and the XY-plane respectively, such that one lies in octant II, one in octant V and one in octant VII. Give the sign pattern that justifies each point.
questions.a: The sizes of x, y and z are 1, 2 and 3. Octant II has signs (-, +, +), giving (-1, 2, 3). Octant V has signs (+, +, -), giving (1, 2, -3). Octant VII has signs (-, -, -), giving (-1, -2, -3).
s: Gives (-1, 2, 3) for octant II with pattern (-, +, +)
Gives (1, 2, -3) for octant V with pattern (+, +, -)
Gives (-1, -2, -3) for octant VII with pattern (-, -, -)

concepts.name: Distance between two points in space
concepts.description: The distance formula in three dimensions, its derivation from a rectangular parallelopiped, and the distance of a point from the origin.
concepts.idea: The segment joining two points is the diagonal of a rectangular box whose edges are the differences of the coordinates, so its length follows from two right angled triangles.
concepts.rule: PQ = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2 + (z2 - z1)^2). The distance of (x, y, z) from the origin is sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2).
concepts.example: For P(1, -3, 4) and Q(-4, 1, 2): PQ = sqrt(25 + 16 + 4) = sqrt(45) = 3 sqrt(5) units.

concepts.name: Using the distance formula: collinear points, figures and sets of points
concepts.description: Applying the distance formula to show points are collinear, to classify triangles and parallelograms, and to find the equation of a set of points satisfying a distance condition.
concepts.idea: Once all the distances between given points are known, they tell us whether the points lie on a line or what figure they form; a distance condition on a variable point (x, y, z) becomes an equation.
concepts.rule: Collinear: the sum of two distances equals the third. Right angled: the square of one side equals the sum of the squares of the other two. Parallelogram (book's method): opposite sides equal; it is a rectangle only if the diagonals are equal. Set of points: write the condition with P(x, y, z), square and simplify.
concepts.example: P(-2, 3, 5), Q(1, 2, 3), R(7, 0, -1): PQ = sqrt(14), QR = 2 sqrt(14), PR = 3 sqrt(14), so PQ + QR = PR and the points are collinear.
